headline: システム is from English system.
Hibana is 火 (hi, “fire”) plus 花 (hana, “flower”).
Shimiru is from Old Japanese 染む (“to dye”), an upper bigrade verb that became upper monograde.
ゼリー is from English jelly.
ジャズ is borrowed from English jazz.
Moriagaru is 盛る (moru) plus 上がる (agaru).
Jodōshi is 助 (“to help”) plus 動詞 (“verb”), literally “helping verb”.
Kokorogakeru is 心 (kokoro, “attention, mind”) plus 掛ける (kakeru, “latch onto”).
デコレーション is borrowed from English decoration.
Daihon is from Sinitic 臺本 (táiběn).
Chōkan is 長 (chō, “chief, leader”) plus 官 (kan, “government official”), either a wasei kango or from Middle Chinese 長官.
Saikai is 再 (“re-”) plus 会 (“meeting”).
In mahi, 麻 is a daiyōji replacing 痲.
Shinjō is 心 (shin, “heart”) plus 情 (jō, “emotion”).
Kaijū is 怪 (kai, “mysterious”) plus 獣 (jū, “beast”).
Kokorobosoi is 心 (kokoro, “heart, feelings”) plus 細い (hosoi, “slender”), with hosoi voiced to bosoi by rendaku.
メーカー is from English maker.
Nozomashii is 望ま (nozoma), the irrealis of 望む (nozomu, “to wish, to hope, to want, to desire”), plus しい (-shī, adjective-forming suffix).
ベース covers “base” and “bass”, and the source borrows both from English.
アクセル is a clipping of アクセラレータ (akuserarēta), from English accelerator.
Ōsuji is 大 (ō-, “big”) plus 筋 (suji, “thread”).
Ikigomu is 意気 (iki, “spirits, enthusiasm”) plus 込む (komu, “to go into; to be full of, to have a lot of”), with komu voiced to gomu by rendaku.
Gairyaku is likely from the Middle Chinese compound 概略, literally “generally, approximately + brief, abbreviated”.
Kyōtei is ultimately traceable to Middle Chinese 協定, but may be a recent Japanese term, attested only since 1877.
Jinsoku is from Middle Chinese 迅速 (MC swinH suwk).
In kokuren, 連 is a daiyōji replacing 聯.
Yūgure is 夕 (yū, “evening”) plus 暮れ (kure, “dusk, nightfall”), with kure voiced to gure by rendaku.
Tsukiru is from Old Japanese, found in the Man'yōshū and spelled phonetically as 都奇 and, in the Nihonshoki kayō, as 豆紀.
Enjiru is a shift from the verb 演ずる (enzuru), as -uru verbs moved to the -iru pattern.
Kanazuchi is 金 (kana, “metal”) plus 槌 (tsuchi, “hammer, mallet”), with tsuchi voiced to zuchi by rendaku.
